Victor went down the stairs happy, terrified, and six months older all at once.

Twenty minutes later, he sat in his car, parked outside his building, trying to collect himself. He knew no one was watching, but he still didn't open the certificate of occupancy.

You couldn't blame people for getting bent out of shape. They took it personally.

An aide tiptoed into Diane's office. He kept his hands raised, holding a folder out before him like a gift. "Sorry I'm late. I thought maybe the committee was in session already."

The aide was Jack Brill. He'd been with her for two years and was the best chief of staff she'd ever had. Brilliant, young, quick with the numbers, and even quicker with his tongue. "No, it just started. They're still sharing feelings."

"I happened to notice the solar gain on the south elevation. You worked it out. Good for you."

"It was a ten-minute fix!"

Diane shook her head. "I can't take the credit. It must be the lighting in here. Nothing I build ever looks that good."

The real issue in the judge's chambers on the sixth floor wasn't solar gain. The project was a block of condominiums near Yale: a white Neo-Georgian monstrosity without any detail or proportion. Most of it had been built by another developer, but two towers facing the street were behind schedule. The architect's arguments interspersed facts and calculations with personal grievances; the Migluary court had signed an agreement deferring the approval of his plans!

Who had ever heard of a judge signing a long-term contract to approve or deny a construction permit? Well, here we are, thought Diane. Living it.

For three years now, the Migluary court had strongly suggested to all who would listen that this was the way the world would have to run. It would save time, money, aggravation, and controversy. Scores of developers had signed on, over her objection.

When Diane and Jack went upstairs, the top judge looked down at them from his chair, and all the other judges and their aides looked down as well. The room was as gloomy as a Friday afternoon staff meeting. Diane sat at the table before the most powerful judges in the city and flipped open her laptop. There was a laptop before each of the other justices, and she made eye contact with the clerk as she typed.

Victor cursed herself for trying to time the heat wave. She had been thrilled when she heard the weatherman's forecast. She had been sure that the inspectors would come either Wednesday or Thursday. And then, Thursday morning – to her horror – she would turn on the local news and hear about the massive three-alarm fire on Superior Street. The anchorwoman would describe how the fire had broken out in the attic of the new Larkspur apartment building during the city-required final inspection. It would still be a terrible tragedy for the building's contractor and owner, but at least it would be an excuse for a certificate of occupancy.

When the inspectors didn't show up on Thursday morning, she turned on the news at four o'clock. On any normal day there would have been masterful weather coverage, with all the anchors at their best: the men in sun-glinting wire-rim glasses, holding a boomer microphone in front of piercing, eyes-adapted-to-climate-change-blue eyes; the blond confections tossing back their heads to let the cameras catch their flowing locks in the breeze.

But not this day. This day they were covering a dog show in God's County. Only one columnist – a man whose true talent was his facility with verbal irony – was allowed to cover weather; he sat in the studio on Thursday afternoon, set between talking about wilted bachelors and the possibilities of a summer cold snap, and did a ten-second live interview with the weatherman.

Mrs. Vandermeer was in the observation lounge across from the TV. The clerks did most of their supervising there so Ms. Vandermeer wouldn't see them. She stood between Haywood spot and the blonde in the window behind them. The center of her mouth hung slack with baloney surprise.

"She said they'd come Thursday or Friday!" she cried, when the cameraman came up behind them to check the lighting.

Ms. Vandermeer always took being laughed at badly. She was startlingly quick to take offense. Once, Ms. Mendoza had even apologized to her – belt-tightening times, she'd admitted, laughing – and she had had to let the woman's error pass amongst the staff.

"It's the midday in temporary event," Mrs. Vandermeer would say whenever she was unhappy about the afternoon's paper. "There's no news in the midday in temporary event."

The decision wasn't a surprise. It was what Victor had always feared, so he was prepared. He smiled at Ms. Ito. "Thank you for your time," he said, and left the room.

The soundproofing was one of his challenges on the Thirteenth Street row houses. For a lot of developers, it was no challenge at all; some of them were happy if the buildings were soundproof between floors, and didn't care about soundproofing between units on the same floor. After all, activists point out, most of the noise in apartment buildings doesn't come from traffic on the street but from slam-bang neighbors—noises too low and too close for soundproof regulations to dampen.

But for Victor it was all or nothing. Once again he got his tools and did the job himself: re-did the masonry with thicker concrete, staggered the studs two feet on center, put diagonal braces on the floors to keep them from bouncing. Then he faced the tape reunion.

He lived at the end of an eight-foot breadboard, laying out lengths of 2-by-4. All day, he lifted a tape and unrolled it, dialed the measurements, laid the tape back down, and let the end snap. In the evening he cut and drilled 2-by-4s and drove screws into the plywood. He finished the heads of the screws exactly level with a single twist each of a 3-inch belt sander. When the work was done, he sanded the plywood, painted it dark forest green, and nailed corner guards to the walls.

There wasn't time for a movie this night. He didn't even take the time to lace up his shoes.

"S', sure," Victor said, quickly.

They stepped into another room, the kind of big, underused space they put in skyscrapers. Ms. Ito handed him a window pole, a long stick with a frog at the end that latched onto the curtains. "Go on, pull it up."

Catching it wrong, Victor dropped the curtain half up. "The attitudes last year that we voted against in the mayoral race?" it read. "Necessity says yes."

Ms. Ito rolled it back into place. "I need your signature on this," she said, offering a letter. Victor had completely forgot he was still in an office, and snatched at it like a rabbit. Later that month, he opened the front door, pushed the button for the opener, and waited for the fire-engine red garage door to crank up with to an ancient groan. He had a clear view of the backyard from the doorway. Wind swirled the leafless dead branches of the willow tree swaying against the night's palpable dark.

When the door was halfway up, Victor believed he heard the heavy slam of boots above. He pulled his key ring out of his back pocket and felt his way toward the switch on the brick wall.

The lights stayed off.

He suspected his brother, who lived upstairs. Victor hated surprise inspections. He hated the way his brother could set them up in a whisper.

Acting without thought, he reached for his flashlight and clicked it on. He pulled the cord of the garage door down in second increments. Light from the door played across the contents of the backyard. He caught movement in the shadows—garbage cans—before seeing the hairline crack between the top of the unsmoothed concrete wall and the bottom of the door. Brown hair with a car number glued to it poked under the motor, where it mounted over the keystone of the archway.

His keys were in the other pocket. Victor found the key to the maintenance room, unlocked the door, and went down to the garage. The door hummed shut as he clicked on the room's florescent light. Beams of light shot out of murk above his head, all the way to the very top of the garage. Below him, Denis Selimovich approached with a curious stare backed by the “get the fuck out . . . ” expression that meant his surprise had been soundly spoiled.

Disjointed footsteps stepped below. There was a cavernous darkness a two-to-four-popscrew driver's weight away from inadvertence. Victor backed up onto the old wooden A-frame ladder, then backed toward the door that let out onto the world above. The metal palms of two work gloves briefly gripped the most uppermost handle, there. Someone held three flashlights by their handles and turned them on with barely a sound. One light shone down by Denis's head, while two others shone down on Victor. A moment later they swung down.

At the middle step, where Victor Sandoval again came in contact with the atmosphere, three circles of haggard tornado-struck faces looked down at him. Two circles' were faceted with protective gear, the third was not.

April, it turned out, wasn't great for business. "Tenderness," he called it. He'd been feeling the full effects for three years, and the economic turnaround that everybody was writing about hadn't touched him. In other trades there were jobs, but they were in towns where he didn't want to live.

Among the things he was tender about were making speeches and sitting in rooms with other people he didn't know.

But that morning he sat in a closed session of City Council with the people who had ruined his life—every one of them out to get him because Victor was doing what all of them were doing, only less discreetly.

Somewhere late last year he'd been sitting in the lobby of a hotel in Santa Fe, reading script on his DVD player, when they'd put out bags for his audition. There were glasses in them and a note: "These are for you. We've altered your audition time—ten minutes from now." The glasses were from Warby Parker and Fitbit headbands, and they'd all been customized with spokes on one side—cheap, even by Victor's standards—to match the braces and canes in front of the chamber in the Board Room.

He'd gone up to audition for upstairs, where he'd been replaced: George Mohammed was now the head of Distress Oversight and Permitting and was back on Tier One. Victor was still on Tier Two, running programs, among them Recap, which he'd started two years before it became mainstream. By the end, nobody cared what he was making. His contract said he could get his old job back if he was on Tier Two, and he now regretted his charm offensive starting five years ago.

"Warby Parker," he'd said when he got upstairs. "I didn't see that coming. Great innovation."

"Am I dating myself?" George had said.

They were on good terms now, but Victor would have told you that George's promotion had been a reward for keeping his mouth shut and not ratting on any of his co-conspirators. Victor already knew what she was going to tell him. She had explained her concerns before, but Victor had thought he could convince her otherwise. But the rules are the rules, she'd said at the start. On paper, Victor's plan wasn't expressly forbidden; there was no rule saying the fire walls had to go right up to the rafters. But most people just burn drywall. Smoke is just as deadly as flames, she'd said, and Victor had had to agree. He avoided her eyes and stared at her gold badge. It was a picture of Ganesha, the Hindu god, from the new subdirectory of the building permit database: Religious Symbols.

Leaving the office, he felt all the food churning in his stomach, the house payments riding up, his family depending on him. In his car he took a flask from his glove box and poured half a glass of tequila.

He went home and found his wife, Jacqui, on the couch, watching the evening news. Not the apartment-house market. Not bankruptcy.

"How was the meeting?" she said. She didn't know, he thought. She was just being polite.

He poured a glass for himself and told her he thought the building was doomed. "But we managed to pay a hundred grand more in labor and subcontracting than we expected. Maybe I can make it up in volume."

"You were drinking," she said. She hadn't even looked at the glass.

"I'm $50,000 in the hole with my brother. He knows it was my fuckup."

He was giddy with the tequila and adrenaline and the building inspector's intuition, but mostly the tequila. He threw his glass on the floor and couldn't hear it break. When he looked up, he was upside down in Jacqui's face, her breath on his lips. He passed out in her arms.

Victor opened his eyes onto the ceiling in the spare bedroom and saw himself still on the couch where Jacqui had picked him up. He was dreaming and not there yet, but the Victor arriving was seeing the one there, grasping the reason for the smirk Jacqui wore while studying her sleeping husband. The first Victor had only been confused and fascinated by the hall-of-mirrors quality of it, how the original Victor managed not even to bother to wake up. He went along for the ride smiling as she rolled him to his bed.

The second Victor never woke up either.

Jacqui only carried him six feet.

Victor drove home alone while it snowed. When he came to a red light, he rolled down his window and heard the air-intake flap whirring for traction. The sound made him think of things slipping out of his control, and he remembered the times his father had said hasta mañana, my friend.

Travel, community, future, neighbors, opportunity: of the six reasons Victor had liked lights-rail so much, the last four seemed shallow now. Maybe his trouble never would have happened if he hadn't fallen in love with the idea that he lived in a dynamic urban region, and maybe it would be better if he stopped pretending he did and got on with his difficult, tangible life.

"Oigayy, cerdo!" someone shouted from a car behind him. Like you, pig. Victor did the alarm-stop in his brain—it was one kind of instinct to risk your life at that moment—kept his hands on the wheel and took a long breath. Behind him the white Subaru was blowing its horn. Was the guy middle-aged, or young and out of college, or fresh from Mexico City? Whoever it was could hardly wait for Victor to get out of the way. Victor moved up to the car ahead of him and turned off on 104th east, and the Subaru climbed right onto the screen in front of him, the gloved hand punching the air system for another quick burst. When Victor looked in his rearview mirror he saw the Subaru pull off. He reached out and dialed Marissa on his cell phone. They had not reconciled. She was the one who had sent him out for milk earlier.

"Hey," she said.

"Hey, babe," Victor said. "I just wanted to call and say I love you."

He took his time getting home. Still a lot to do before Christmas, he thought.

He drove the building site in his Silverado, and pulled up alongside the one-story shed that housed the elevators and the laundry room. He had never met this Gallagher, and didn't even know what department he represented, but something in Ito's note bothered him. Supervisors aren't normally asked for confirmation of an inspection. He had a feeling she intended to stand him on the floor and let him talk himself right out of a certificate.

Gallagher was waiting for him on the sidewalk, dressed in jeans and sneakers, with a bulging nylon satchel and a blond ponytail tied back at the nape of his neck.

"Mr. Sandoval. Good to meet you. I'm Michael Gallagher."

His nod was tentative. He didn't shake hands. "Why are we here?"

"Well . . . the new carpet went in this morning. And if your inspector follows me up in an elevator, she'll be able to check it from the private roof. She seemed drop-dead certain about that."

On the way, Victor recited the mechanisms—wheels and threads and lift cables—powering the German-made elevator in Gallagher's bulging bag. You don't build the one-story suburbs that fed Victor's shingle siding business without knowing about elevators, or their history. Gallagher could recite it as well.

"McGuire installed 23,000 elevators in New York City, from 1857 to 1925, and the company name went up a lot farther along its track record than yours has, Mr. Sandoval."

"The permit was drawn for the Westinghouse," he said, irritated.

"It was. But 10,000 of those McGuire elevators are still in service."

The new home elevators, rated for light use in four-story buildings, weren't even made in America, Gallagher told him. They were built in Lutheran Germany and designed by a Dutch engineering firm that specialized in home machinery—from dishwasher pumps to light-rail turntables.

"You know those glass boxes at street level with the turntables on top?"

"Yes. Why?"

"I work there. The design makes me nervous. I'd much rather trust my life to a five-year-old technology developed by an elevator company than a ten-year-old turntable designed by a table-company."

It was a grid with days, weeks, and inspection stations arrayed down the left, and times crossed across the top. In the appropriate boxes he was to write a brief record of whatever was going on that hour. It was Friday morning, and he dutifully recorded the tasks that were completed.

Across the hall, Victor Sandoval's company was installing wiring, painting, and finishing cabinetry. All of that work would go on the building's sign-in sheet. When done, it would count as prerelease inspections, satisfying, among other requirements, that only licensed workers be involved in finishing work.

Some work wouldn't go on any log at all. But before very long it would be included in a climbing wall of red tape, bolted to the siding of a building that would be encircled by a chain-link fence. Victor laughed until tears came to his eyes. He turned it over quickly so his top-heavy frame wouldn't topple off the chair. On the back he wrote: "SORRY. DO YOU WANT THAT IN CAPITAL LETTERS?"

After he left she watched him from the window: the pale Irish skin, the aging blond hair, the wide, knotted frame in a sweat-streaked white T-shirt. There was something about his shape, almost contrite, she mused, like a Boy Scout who's trespassing. She was familiar with Victor Sandoval, and she knew why she was familiar: The court documents on his file with health records and social services filled a three-inch binder.

He was fifty-three years old and had been "homeless" for thirty. She often argued with herself about that paradoxical status. In 1938, in the early months of the Great Depression, with dominoes falling in Europe and poverty and unemployment sweeping the United States, Congress passed the Federal Housing Act, a landmark law aimed at creating decent, affordable housing for working families. The act established the Federal Housing Administration, which provided mortgage insurance to banks that would make loans for suburban housing projects that met certain requirements. And it authorized studies of America's housing needs.

Two years later, the Housing and Urban Development Survey was published. Researchers who'd traveled the country discovered that one third of all Americans lived in "slums," defective or substandard housing. This just in time for World War II. Housing came under tight rationing, and few new homes were built. People stayed put and fixed what they could. For twenty years afterward, the government continued to publish reports with dire titles like The Housing Shortfall and An Analysis of Alaska's Low-Income Housing Problems.

By the end of the 1960s, perhaps because of the Centennial, America's Congressional delegation had been transformed into a small industry of amateur statisticians. If it was proposed, it was quantified. If it was quantified, it had to be known to Congress. To support this work, agencies were created, among them the U.S. Census Bureau in 1800 and the Department of Commerce in 1875, both of which had published population counts since before the time of Lincoln. In the 1970s, however, the Census Bureau not only moved control of its data centers to Sacramento and New Jersey, it also moved its management structure into the new Office of Management and Budget, with two layers of Republican appointees. Political appointees, one can only presume, are the new professionals in the bureaucracy.

The 1980 census, a kind of crash course for a series of crunches, counted 226.5 million people. The classroom was still cool and quiet. Nervous giggling and scraping metal chairs was the only sound.

On each side of the room were empty desks with paper school district ID cards taped to the front, photograph and name on one side and typed instructions on the other.

As the students filed in, Mr. Oak finished crossing something off a handwritten matrix in his spiral notebook: N-20. "Research Order," he would tell future students about this matrix, "is always done before name cards are sorted by gender and displayed around the room." Behind the desk he was using in front of the blackboard was a brown paper grocery sack on top of another grocery sack, on top of another, down to a new sack on the floor.

Last period, during "Research Order," the students had found out who they'd been matched with, by reading one ID card with a statement about their partner on the back—this was somebody you could tell right away—but they hadn't yet seen each other or heard each other's names.

Samuel Clark was sitting in the front row, second from the left, the only boy with hair outside his shorts. He'd been married as often as anybody else in the class, and on at least one of those occasions his partner had been his current partner's former partner.

He picked up the ID card that said MY PARTNER who ever it was liked the movies because his favorite class was video art. Because I'm a journalist my pay scale, per se, varies. Thinking like an economist — and in our trade, as it has now come to be called, you learn to do exactly that -- provides a cane in the dark.

Among the seeds of doubt a New York economy plants in its clutch, there is one you (a fellow member of the middle class or, possibly, an inquiring visitor) may find particularly unsettling: the weight of what you pass as success.

A family-labor income in the low six figures in a city where the rent for a studio large enough to vacuum without banging elbows is $800 a month appears impressive from any but the highest rung of the local ladder. Nevertheless, even in a job market where driving cars with fake engines has a generational appeal, and where a salesman at the Mitsubishi Galleria deflects questions of fun, work, quality of life by stiff-arming the interviewer off the premises, family wage cards with a 09 stamp seem too easily spent.

A careful study — one I must leave to other investigators — would probably reveal a significant drop-off in good restaurants, comparable houses, group activity, artist pay and time, air-conditioning, and, depending on the level of hair-splitting, shoe shine, among the emerging middle classes in New York.

Victor checked the trailer's tarp every few miles. He had visions of the wind whipping the drywall into tatters, or the metal studs banging into each other until every flange was bent. In the orange twilight he drove the trailer at fifty miles an hour to the Larkspur site and backed it into the loading dock. He and the subcontractor wrestled the loads down to the workroom one at a time. Victor worked until midnight, trying to convince himself that he had saved something.

In the morning he went into the attic with a ladder and a pair of utility knives, and over the next three days he cut out every fire wall that he had ever built. Perhaps it was a way to start again, he told himself. He left the scrap pieces on the lawn and watched the wind blow them into piles against the chain-link fence. *

"You may occupy the building," she said, "provisionally."

Above the box for her signature, she had written:

Failure to correct noted deficiencies within the one-week probationary period will result in immediate revocation of this certificate and shutdown of the occupancy permit. ALL PERSONS WILL BE REQUIRED TO EVACUATE THE PREMISES. Penalties include criminal prosecution.

She looked up at him. "I'm giving you one week, Victor. That's it."

Victor stared at the paper in silence.

"It's not over," she said. "None of it's over until I come back and verify the corrections."

Victor nodded.

"One last thing," she said. "Unless you have a real death wish, don't go back up into that attic. The insulation there is loose, and it's highly combustible. They sweep sawdust in there when they built the place, and it's never been cleaned out. If there's a fire in one unit, the whole building could go." She paused. "Next time I might not go easy on you."

He had started to stand up, but he sat down again. "Can you tell me what I have to do?"

She looked at her watch. "You have to take all that loose insulation out of the attic. You have to install proper fire stops between the units and at the intersection of all the wall penetrations on each floor. You have to rewire half the building because your circuits are overloaded and outdated--that was easy to miss, I'll give you that. You have to upgrade the emergency lighting in the stairwells.

"Your dishwasher intake is discharging raw sewage into the alley; you'll have to pipe it to the sanitary main. And if I were you, I'd junk the boilers and install gas heat. Those oil burners are December 1973 technology."

He heard her talking, but all he could think about was insurance. His contractor had the job only to the studs. The rest had been hustled off to subcontractors who couldn't be found anymore; the ones who were still in business had all given him estimates three months ago. The prices had gone up since then. He would have to begin again, from scratch.

He thought of the deposit he'd accepted from the buyers of unit 23, the young couple who needed a place for their baby. He would have to tell them it wasn't ready yet. They'd been waiting six months.

"I was trying to save you time," she said. "I'm sorry that didn't come through clearly enough. Next time, you should read the code yourself, or hire someone who can. There's always a phone number on the first page of every booklet."

Victor was looking at the first page of the building code, the chapter on Fire Resistive Construction. He'd never seen it before. He hadn't even known the book existed.

"I just want you to understand," he said, "this isn't--this isn't something small. Even if I did appeal--if I lost the appeal, I'd have to tear the whole building down. You know what that would cost?"

Ms. Ito tapped on her desk with one finger. "You passed this project. You signed off on all the inspection tickets. You had plenty of chances to look inside the walls."

"But I trusted people," Victor said. "You can't trust anyone these days." Upstairs in the attic, he pictured his brother's savings smoldering behind the thin new drywall. He pictured the hard-hatted men he'd bought coffee for every morning, losing their jobs. He pictured the families who were going to move in, where they would end up instead. For the first time, he thought about whose face he would have to see across the desk from him when he tried to borrow money for his funeral. Then he thought about calling the bank and negotiating the loan, letting them have the building for what it would be worth--a hole in the ground.

Could you ask for another inspection? he asked himself, another appeal? Could you go through all the lawyers and all the courts only to end up on your knees, begging someone to lend you enough money to knock the building down? Had everything just been a mistake? Had he fundamentally misunderstood, at a cellular level, how to do business in this city?

At 4:10 a fire broke out in the attic between 311 and 312. Victor and the superintendent entered by the back of 311, and quickly found the blaze. They tried to put it out with a couple of extinguishers to no avail. They ran downstairs to call 911, and by then one unit was fully engulfed.

Afterward, Victor went back to the building and walked through the wreckage. Downstairs, an elegant widow from Monte Amici told him she'd been living out of boxes for the last month, waiting to move, and that if he'd been honest with her, she wouldn't have signed a lease.

Victor thought about that and then he thought about the future. When the smoke cleared, he'd be out on the street, with no apartment, no house, and no job. And a wife and four kids. So he went around the scorched apartments asking everyone to sign a two-page document. It said that, in exchange for a gift of a Samsung LCD TV, a new tenant agreed to drop all claims against the building's owner, Victor Sandoval.

By nightfall only Unit 311 was still empty. An envelope was slipped under the door. Inside the letter started, "Dear Mr. Sandoval," and ended, "Sincerely, Ms. Ito." It said that in seventeen months it would be too late for him to deny what he'd done. When she has sworn into office, Diane Ito will enjoy telling Victor Sandoval the penalty for arson was twenty years to life.

"Don't pick things up that look like money," the woman said. Mark looked up. For the first time he noticed the woman. She wore mannish clothes and had a head that looked like a butcher's block.

"Pardon me?"

The woman's mouth stayed open. She looked around, in every direction, as if some invisible person were speaking to her. The silence was absolute.

"I have no idea what you're talking about," he said.

Suddenly the old woman smiled, like an alligator.

"I only thought I saw you pick up something that looked like money."

"But I didn't pick any money up. Not here, not anywhere."

Mark hadn't used cash in years. He had two credit cards and he paid for everything with them. Today's meal was courtesy of the American Bar Association.

"Whatever, whatever." The woman smacked her lips.

"Are we talking around my table while I'm eating?" the man asked.

They were. The man slapped his palms down where they clattered on the tabletop, three times. The woman leaned back in her chair. "Have you no manners at all?" she said, sounding much younger now that the alligator was gone. But the young woman was also mean, much worse than the old one. "My name is Marmee. What's yours?"

He hesitated not for a moment. "Mark."

Neither her parents nor his had known what the name of the boy in the attic had been or when he had lived there. They had only known that he had hidden from the three women who had chased him everywhere he went. The boy had been afraid of his own voice so he had taken a vow of silence every day for four hundred years.

Mark wasn't a reader. He had never read a book from cover to cover. If he had, he'd know that all fairy tales have a moral at the end.

"The moral of the story," Mark had once told a woman between the bedsheets, "is the obvious."

That one.

Teleterra itself was nothing but a research facility and a spaceport. Nobody lived there. The main building was a big orange cylinder, and the spaceport was even bigger. All the people who worked there lived in four small towns on the edge of the triangle, at the end of the space shuttle run.

No one tended to stay. With the shuttle, it was just as easy to commute a hundred miles as a mile. People worked in Orion or Rexford or Shreveport, and rented an apartment or got married or built a house and then moved on. The real estate agents found few customers.

At least they did for a while.

Then Leng Corporation announced the plans for Luna City. Their vision, about three stories tall and sixty feet wide, showed a town with everything you'd want in a traditional living-neighborhood. Shoppers' Row had the fish market, the butchers, the art supply store, and the optometrist. Exquisite coffee shops and restaurants also borderered the indoor garden. There was an amphitheater. There was a church. The whole thing, the two colonels noted in their reports, was round.

The novelty of the project wasn't so much the idea of the town that levitated. It was the idea that a town could levitate while it brought itself down to earth. The company says that while the town was building itself the much smaller local communities that had been developed around it would give the main city a living, breathing foundation, which in turn would see the arrival of more and more people.

In the end the town would take shape according to its program. However, both colonels insisted that it could be shaped by people. No two people head in exactly the same direction - even in deep space - and so the colonels insisted there was room for variation, and that the effect of myriad small variations would then alter the course of the journey.

And so it was up to the people to arrive first. When Leng Corporation donated five million dollars to the research into space exploration it came with a condition encouraging volunteerism in teleterra. No, it's not okay. His head throbbed, each beat like a fist. He pushed himself to his feet.

Wendy was pouring juice into glasses. She turned and saw him. She paused, as if intrigued, the pitcher balanced in her fist. Crumb specks powdered her blouse. "Did you have a good sleep?"

The room was crowded with boxes and furniture squeezed into narrow spaces. "I love you," he said. It was the wrong thing to say, but the only thing he could dredge from the watery sinkhole in his heart.

Wendy put the pitcher down. "Is there something wrong?"

"Are you two okay?" he asked. Nobody answered. His children hung on under the half-closed eyes of their mother. The children were seven and nine. Behind the specter of the nursery room he envisioned the long reach of empty nights, rooms moved through because it seemed necessary, days that dripped with mindless work like water from a leaking roof.

"The rolls are almost ready," Wendy said, moving to the kitchen window, pulling the blinds up. "Any minute now they'll be done."
